When the Moon and Sun align

This rare sight — a total solar eclipse — was photographed in San Millán de los Caballeros, Spain, on Aug. 12.

The Sun is 400 times wider than the Moon, but in a cosmic coincidence, it's also 400 times further away. This means that they appear to be the same size in our sky — and when the Moon passes in front, it can perfectly block the Sun.

Credit: NASA

What do you see in this photo by @NASAWebb? A bird? An elephant? A giraffe?
 
This is Webb’s infrared view of part of the Carina Nebula, a star-forming region also home to the Cosmic Cliffs, which was one of the first images released by Webb. Here Webb captures a different aspect of Carina: a feature called the Treasure Chest, which is an object known as a cometary globule.
 
A cometary globule is an isolated cloud of gas and dust with a dense, dark head and a sweeping tail. These clouds often somewhat resemble comets, but the Treasure Chest looks distinctly like a wooden chest with its lid wide open… or the plumes of a space chicken. Inside is a compact cluster of massive, young stars wrapped up in dust. Some of these baby stars are surrounded by disks that may one day produce planets.

Hold the dots and scroll to switch between Hubble and Roman’s vision. 👀
 
Later this month, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will launch to begin surveying the cosmos. Here, you’re looking at a mock comparison of @NASAHubble vs. Roman’s field of view.
 
The Roman Space Telescope’s main superpower is its wide vision. At over 100 times the size of Hubble’s vision but with the same crisp clarity, Roman can capture sweeping views of the universe with each picture.
 
How does Roman’s uniquely large perspective come in handy? The universe is so vast that finding targets of study can be like searching for a needle in a big, cosmic haystack. Roman’s ultra-wide vision will help scientists pinpoint these needles, or new objects of scientific interest. Then, our other space telescopes can study those targets in-depth. Teamwork!
 
Credit: L. Hustak (STScI)

A dance of darkness and light

This composite image shows the total solar eclipse from beginning to end, as seen in San Millán de los Caballeros, Spain on Aug. 12, 2026.

While eclipses are beautiful and magical to experience, they're also a great opportunity for science. Total solar eclipses are particularly important because they allow scientists to see a part of the Sun’s atmosphere known as the corona. The corona is too faint to see except when the bright light of the Sun is blocked.

Studying the corona is key to answering important questions about how heat and energy are transferred from the Sun out into the solar wind, the constant stream of particles that the Sun spews into the solar system.

Credit: NASA

Coming out of my shell

One thousand years ago, a star exploded — and it was so bright that it lit up the daytime sky for weeks. The supernova hurled much of the star's material into space, creating a shell of debris that continues to expand even today.

This supernova remnant (officially known as SN 1006) is roughly the size of the full moon in Earth's sky, but most of its shell only shows up with radio or X-ray vision — not visible light. This image combines data across a number of frequencies, collected by @nasahubble, @nasachandraxray, and several Earth-based telescopes.
